questions.question: A patient with a remote MI survives documented VF. There is no acute infarction, culprit ischemia, drug toxicity or electrolyte explanation after evaluation. LVEF is 42%, and meaningful functional survival beyond one year is expected. Which strategy is appropriate?
options: Offer an ICD for secondary prevention after shared assessment of benefits and burdens
Defer ICD because EF is above the usual primary-prevention threshold
Require inducible sustained VT at EPS before offering an ICD
Use chronic amiodarone as an equivalent substitute for ICD protection
questions.explanation:
Secondary-Prevention ICD After Resuscitated VF

Correct answer: Offer an ICD for secondary prevention after shared assessment of benefits and burdens

Distinguish a Prior Event From Predicted Future Risk

**An eligible survivor of VF or hemodynamically poorly tolerated VT without a reversible cause has a secondary-prevention ICD indication.** The EF thresholds used to select event-free primary-prevention patients answer a different question.

Confirm the rhythm and investigate acute ischemia, infarction, electrolyte abnormalities, proarrhythmic medication and other potentially reversible contributors. A single abnormal laboratory value does not automatically prove that it fully explains the event.

Remote infarct scar remains an important persistent substrate even when global EF is above thirty-five percent. Preserved or mildly reduced EF does not erase the significance of documented VF.

Assess Reversibility and Expected Benefit Carefully

**Consider functional survival, competing disease, device complications and patient preferences before implantation.** The device can terminate future ventricular arrhythmia but does not treat HF progression or prevent every cause of death.

VT/VF during the early acute-MI period has a different assessment from late scar-related events. Do not apply a primary-prevention waiting interval as a blanket reason to delay every secondary-prevention indication.

Continue coronary and HF treatment and consider antiarrhythmics or ablation when recurrent arrhythmia requires suppression. Review the need for pacing, ATP or CRT before choosing a device system. A successful ablation does not universally remove secondary-prevention risk, although selected tolerated-VT scenarios have disease- and guideline-specific alternatives that differ from this VF survivor. Discuss inappropriate shocks, lead or pocket complications, follow-up, generator replacement and future goals of care. When an event is convincingly reversible, the decision may change, but uncertainty about residual substrate requires individualized review rather than an automatic label of cured. The supplied absence of an acute explanation and good expected survival make device protection appropriate despite EF of forty-two percent.

Defer ICD because EF is above the usual primary-prevention threshold: Primary-prevention EF cut-offs do not exclude an eligible survivor of VF without a reversible cause. A prior malignant event supplies a different indication.

Require inducible sustained VT at EPS before offering an ICD: EPS has selected diagnostic and risk-assessment uses, but documented VF without a reversible cause does not require an additional inducibility result to establish the secondary-prevention pathway.

Use chronic amiodarone as an equivalent substitute for ICD protection: Amiodarone can reduce recurrent ventricular arrhythmia in selected patients but is not an equivalent routine substitute for indicated secondary-prevention ICD therapy. Drug and device roles are complementary.

ESC ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.12.012

questions.question: Six months after MI and PCI, a patient remains NYHA class II with LVEF 32% despite chronic maximally tolerated guideline-directed therapy. There has been no sustained ventricular arrhythmia. Meaningful survival beyond one year is expected. Under US guidance, which strategy is appropriate?
options: Require inducible VT at EPS because no spontaneous arrhythmia has occurred
Wait for sustained VT before offering an ICD
Require LVEF at or below thirty percent because all ischemic indications use that threshold
Offer an ICD for primary prevention after shared decision-making
questions.explanation:
Primary-Prevention ICD in Chronic Ischemic Cardiomyopathy

Correct answer: Offer an ICD for primary prevention after shared decision-making

Match EF to Symptoms and Treatment History

**US HF guidance recommends a primary-prevention ICD for eligible ischemic patients with LVEF at most 35%, NYHA II–III symptoms and chronic GDMT.** Meaningful survival beyond one year and the relevant post-MI and revascularization intervals are required.

A distinct recommendation uses LVEF at most 30% with NYHA I symptoms after MI. Do not transfer that stricter EF threshold to every symptomatic patient.

Confirm that EF remains reduced after an adequate treatment period and is measured reliably. An early acute-illness value is not equivalent to persistent chronic dysfunction.

Evaluate Device Benefit Within Comprehensive HF Care

**An ICD prevents selected arrhythmic deaths; it does not replace therapies that improve ventricular function and reduce HF events.** Continue appropriate neurohormonal and SGLT2-inhibitor treatment and coronary prevention.

Consider competing mortality, frailty, renal disease and patient goals. A numerical EF criterion does not guarantee net benefit when serious comorbidity limits functional survival.

Review QRS duration, bundle-branch pattern, rhythm and pacing needs to determine whether CRT or another device configuration is also indicated. An ICD indication alone does not automatically establish CRT eligibility. Discuss shocks, infection, lead complications, generator replacement and follow-up. This patient is six months after MI and PCI, so the supplied timing avoids premature prophylactic implantation and allows assessment of persistent dysfunction. New sustained arrhythmia, syncope or clinical deterioration would require a separate urgent assessment rather than waiting for the next routine EF measurement. The purpose of primary prevention is to intervene before a malignant event in a group with demonstrated benefit, not to wait for a monitor to document the event one hopes to prevent.

Require inducible VT at EPS because no spontaneous arrhythmia has occurred: Selected ischemic NSVT pathways use inducibility, but the supplied EF, symptom and treatment criteria establish a separate recommendation that does not require EPS.

Wait for sustained VT before offering an ICD: A prior sustained event defines a secondary-prevention pathway. An appropriate primary-prevention indication does not require the patient first to experience that event.

Require LVEF at or below thirty percent because all ischemic indications use that threshold: The thirty-percent threshold applies to a specific NYHA class I post-MI recommendation. NYHA II–III patients can qualify with EF at or below thirty-five percent when other criteria are met.

Timing of Prophylactic ICD Assessment After MI

Correct answer: Optimize treatment and reassess EF after the required post-MI and postrevascularization recovery intervals

questions.question: Which interpretation of DINAMIT and IRIS best explains why high early post-MI sudden-death risk does not by itself justify routine immediate prophylactic ICD implantation?
options: The results exclude an ICD indication for any later post-MI survivor
The devices failed to terminate ventricular arrhythmias in the early post-MI period
The trials established improved overall survival but poor cost-effectiveness
Early ICD implantation reduced arrhythmic or sudden deaths but did not improve overall survival in the studied populations
questions.explanation:
Early Post-MI ICD Trials and Competing Mortality

Correct answer: Early ICD implantation reduced arrhythmic or sudden deaths but did not improve overall survival in the studied populations

Risk Prediction Is Not Proof of Intervention Benefit

**DINAMIT and IRIS evaluated prophylactic ICD implantation early after MI in selected high-risk patients.** Both failed to demonstrate an overall survival advantage despite fewer arrhythmic or sudden deaths.

Nonarrhythmic deaths were more frequent in the ICD groups, offsetting the cause-specific reduction. This illustrates competing risk; it does not establish that each prevented arrhythmic death was causally converted into another type of death.

A device can interrupt VT/VF without preventing progressive pump failure, recurrent ischemic injury or other major causes of mortality during early recovery.

Apply the Findings to the Correct Decision

**Routine primary-prevention timing permits treatment and reassessment before selecting persistent-risk patients.** The standard US framework includes at least forty days after MI and ninety days after revascularization when applicable.

Continue active HF and coronary treatment during recovery, and reassess EF and symptoms rather than treating the waiting interval as a period without care. Temporary protection is a separate individualized question.

Do not use these trials to deny secondary-prevention assessment after a documented nonreversible malignant arrhythmia or to ignore necessary pacing. Conversely, a low early EF alone does not prove that immediate implantation improves survival. Evaluate the actual population, comparator and endpoint before transferring trial findings into an examination answer. Explain to patients that high risk can coexist with uncertainty or lack of benefit from a particular intervention at a particular time. Later persistent dysfunction may support an ICD after recovery, while substantial improvement can remove the original primary-prevention rationale. Meaningful survival, competing comorbidity and patient preference remain relevant at the reassessment.

The results exclude an ICD indication for any later post-MI survivor: The timing and selection differ from chronic primary-prevention trials and secondary-prevention indications. An early negative trial does not invalidate later implantation when established criteria are met.

The devices failed to terminate ventricular arrhythmias in the early post-MI period: Lack of an overall survival advantage does not mean the devices had no antiarrhythmic efficacy. Cause-specific deaths and total mortality must be distinguished.

The trials established improved overall survival but poor cost-effectiveness: The limitation was not simply economic. The randomized early-implant strategies did not demonstrate the overall survival benefit required to support routine prophylactic use in those populations.

questions.question: A 56-year-old with nonischemic DCM remains NYHA II with LVEF 30% after six months of maximally tolerated GDMT. There is no transient cause, QRS is narrow and meaningful survival beyond one year is expected. Under US 2022 HF guidance, which plan is appropriate?
options: Require a broad QRS before considering an ICD
Exclude ICD because the cardiomyopathy is nonischemic
Offer primary-prevention ICD treatment after individualized discussion
Require documented sustained VT before considering any device
questions.explanation:
Primary-Prevention ICD in Nonischemic DCM

Correct answer: Offer primary-prevention ICD treatment after individualized discussion

Use the Explicit Guideline Framework

**US 2022 HF guidance recommends ICD treatment in eligible nonischemic DCM with LVEF at most 35%, NYHA II–III symptoms and chronic GDMT when meaningful survival beyond one year is expected.** Confirm that the dysfunction persists after adequate treatment.

Assess reversible causes, including tachycardia-mediated or toxic disease, and investigate etiology with appropriate imaging and genetic evaluation. A disease-specific high-risk genotype or scar phenotype can influence decisions beyond a single EF threshold.

The six-month treated history distinguishes this case from a newly diagnosed patient whose EF may improve promptly with therapy. Narrow QRS means there is no supplied conventional CRT indication, not that defibrillation protection is ineffective.

Discuss Heterogeneous Benefit and Competing Risks

**Nonischemic DCM is a diverse group, and trial findings must be interpreted alongside age, substrate and competing mortality.** DANISH did not show a significant overall all-cause mortality reduction in its studied population, while reducing sudden death.

This result does not erase the named US recommendation or prove identical benefit for every patient. European recommendation strength and disease-specific risk approaches differ, so identify the framework when writing or answering a question.

Continue comprehensive HF treatment and reassess symptoms, renal function and expected survival. Discuss inappropriate shocks, infection, lead complications and future generator changes rather than presenting implantation as a purely numerical decision. Severe comorbidity limiting survival can change the balance despite a qualifying EF. Incorporate the patient’s goals and consider advanced HF options when appropriate. A later EF improvement, new arrhythmia or newly identified genetic diagnosis can alter follow-up decisions, but should be evaluated from current evidence rather than an assumption that every nonischemic heart behaves alike.

Require a broad QRS before considering an ICD: QRS duration influences CRT selection, not every ICD indication. A narrow QRS does not negate the supplied primary-prevention criteria.

Exclude ICD because the cardiomyopathy is nonischemic: US guidance includes eligible nonischemic DCM with EF at or below thirty-five percent, NYHA II–III symptoms and chronic GDMT. Ischemic etiology is not required for this recommendation.

Require documented sustained VT before considering any device: That would convert a primary-prevention decision into waiting for a secondary-prevention event. Persistent qualifying dysfunction and symptoms can support implantation without prior sustained VT.

questions.question: Which statement accurately summarizes the original DANISH trial of prophylactic ICD therapy in nonischemic systolic HF?
options: ICD treatment significantly reduced all-cause mortality without reducing sudden death
ICD treatment reduced sudden cardiac death but did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality in the overall trial population
ICD treatment and control were proven equivalent for survival
The study compared CRT-defibrillators with medical treatment that excluded CRT
questions.explanation:
Interpreting DANISH Without Overstating a Negative Endpoint

Correct answer: ICD treatment reduced sudden cardiac death but did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality in the overall trial population

Keep the Primary and Secondary Outcomes Distinct

**DANISH enrolled 1116 patients with nonischemic systolic HF and LVEF at most 35%.** Patients received an ICD or usual care, with CRT in approximately 58% of each group.

At median follow-up of 67.6 months, all-cause mortality was 21.6% with ICD versus 23.4% in controls: HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.68–1.12. This did not establish a significant reduction in the primary endpoint.

Sudden cardiac death was 4.3% versus 8.2%, HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.31–0.82. The cause-specific benefit should not disappear from the interpretation merely because the primary endpoint was negative.

Translate the Trial Through Patient Selection

**Competing nonarrhythmic mortality affects the potential overall benefit of defibrillator protection.** Age, comorbidity, HF severity and contemporary treatment influence the proportion of deaths an ICD can prevent.

Age-related analyses inform discussion but do not create a universal age prohibition. Subgroup or extended-follow-up findings require their own attribution rather than silently replacing the original randomized primary result.

The trial does not prove absence of benefit in every nonischemic phenotype or invalidate all guideline recommendations. Genetic risk, myocardial scar and arrhythmic history can identify patients unlike the average trial participant. Conversely, an EF threshold should not override severe competing disease that limits meaningful survival. Discuss procedural and long-term device harms as well as potential prevention of sudden death, and continue GDMT and indicated CRT. A statistically nonsignificant all-cause result is neither proof of equivalence nor evidence that the device cannot terminate malignant arrhythmia. Explicitly name the outcome when describing benefit so patients and examinees do not confuse sudden-death prevention with a guaranteed overall survival extension.

ICD treatment significantly reduced all-cause mortality without reducing sudden death: This reverses the trial’s findings. Sudden death was reduced, while the overall all-cause mortality primary endpoint was not significantly lower.

ICD treatment and control were proven equivalent for survival: Failure to demonstrate superiority is not an equivalence result. The confidence interval includes different plausible effects and must be interpreted with trial design and population.

The study compared CRT-defibrillators with medical treatment that excluded CRT: CRT was used in a substantial proportion of both groups when indicated. The comparison tested added defibrillator protection on contemporary background care rather than CRT versus its absence.

questions.question: A patient with DCM has LVEF 44% despite treatment, unexplained syncope and significant LGE on CMR. No sustained VT has been documented. Under the ESC 2022 multiparametric framework, which next approach is most appropriate?
options: Consider primary-prevention ICD assessment because EF below fifty percent and two specified risk factors are present
Exclude ICD assessment because EF is above thirty-five percent
Treat LGE alone as a mandatory ICD indication regardless of the rest of the phenotype
Require a pathogenic variant before clinical and imaging risk factors can be used
questions.explanation:
DCM Risk Assessment Above the Conventional EF Threshold

Correct answer: Consider primary-prevention ICD assessment because EF below fifty percent and two specified risk factors are present

Integrate the Risk Features Rather Than EF Alone

**ESC 2022 advises considering an ICD in DCM or hypokinetic nondilated cardiomyopathy with LVEF below 50% and at least two specified risk factors.** Unexplained syncope and LGE on CMR satisfy two features in this stem.

The framework also includes inducible sustained monomorphic VT and selected pathogenic variants, particularly PLN, FLNC or RBM20. LMNA-associated disease additionally has a gene-specific risk-calculation pathway.

Confirm that the syncope remains unexplained after appropriate assessment and that LGE is reliably interpreted. Nonspecific dizziness or an imaging artefact should not be promoted into a qualifying risk factor.

Recognize Disease-Specific and Genetic Nuance

**The 2023 cardiomyopathy guideline further emphasizes high-risk genetic backgrounds and scar phenotypes that can justify assessment above an EF of 35%.** Variant type, expression, arrhythmia and family history affect interpretation.

questions.question: An ICD candidate has recurrent monomorphic VT reliably terminated by ATP and also needs ongoing bradycardia pacing. Which device-selection statement is most appropriate?
options: A conventional standalone subcutaneous ICD does not provide the required ATP and chronic pacing functions
A standalone subcutaneous ICD provides equivalent chronic bradycardia pacing
A standalone subcutaneous ICD supplies routine ATP for monomorphic VT
Avoiding an intravascular lead removes the need to assess pacing requirements
questions.explanation:
Subcutaneous Versus Transvenous ICD Capabilities

Correct answer: A conventional standalone subcutaneous ICD does not provide the required ATP and chronic pacing functions

Select the System for the Required Therapies

**A conventional standalone S-ICD provides defibrillation without routine ATP, chronic bradycardia pacing or CRT.** It can be appropriate when those functions are neither needed nor anticipated.

Transvenous systems can provide bradycardia pacing and ATP, with CRT-defibrillator configurations when resynchronization is indicated. Not every transvenous ICD automatically provides CRT.

The repeated ATP-responsive rhythm and existing bradycardia requirement make a standalone S-ICD a poor match here, irrespective of whether it can deliver an effective shock.

Balance Capabilities Against Long-Term Burden

**Subcutaneous placement avoids an intravascular defibrillator lead but retains pocket, sensing and shock-related risks.** Assess ECG screening, anatomy, infection history, vascular access and likely future pacing needs.

Newer substernal extravascular ICDs and modular combinations with leadless pacing are distinct systems. Their capabilities and availability must not be conflated with a conventional standalone S-ICD.

An independent pacemaker or modular approach may solve selected problems, but adds compatibility, follow-up and procedural considerations rather than making all systems interchangeable. Discuss ATP benefit, potential acceleration, shocks, lead failure and extraction implications. A younger patient without pacing needs may prioritize avoiding intravascular hardware, while a patient with recurrent slow monomorphic VT may derive substantial benefit from ATP. Reassess the expected disease course and preferences before implantation. The correct question is which system can deliver the patient’s required therapies with an acceptable burden, not which device is newest or has the fewest leads.

A standalone subcutaneous ICD provides equivalent chronic bradycardia pacing: Brief postshock pacing capability is not equivalent to dependable chronic bradycardia support. The required function must be assessed before choosing the system.

A standalone subcutaneous ICD supplies routine ATP for monomorphic VT: Conventional standalone S-ICD systems do not provide ATP. A system capable of pacing-mediated termination is relevant when this repeatedly useful therapy is needed.

Avoiding an intravascular lead removes the need to assess pacing requirements: Extravascular placement can reduce particular lead-related burdens, but does not make missing therapeutic capabilities irrelevant. Device selection must address both defibrillation and pacing needs.

Multisociety ICD/CRT/pacing appropriate use criteria, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.023

questions.question: A primary-prevention ICD patient has therapies for short self-terminating episodes and rapidly conducted atrial arrhythmia. There is no known clinically important slow VT. Which programming review is most appropriate?
options: Shorten detection intervals to treat every brief fast rhythm sooner
Review longer detection, appropriate rate thresholds, discrimination and ATP settings for the documented rhythms
Disable ATP so every detected ventricular episode receives a shock
Raise the therapy threshold without reviewing stored rhythms or prior clinical VT
questions.explanation:
Programming to Reduce Avoidable ICD Therapy

Correct answer: Review longer detection, appropriate rate thresholds, discrimination and ATP settings for the documented rhythms

Detection Is a Treatment Decision

**Rate and duration thresholds determine which episodes receive therapy.** Longer detection can permit nonsustained arrhythmia to stop, while discrimination can reduce treatment of supraventricular rhythms.

Review stored electrograms to identify the actual reason for therapy. AF, other SVT, oversensing and true ventricular episodes require different corrective actions.

ATP can terminate monomorphic reentry without a painful shock, but can occasionally accelerate VT. Program sequences and shock backup according to rhythm characteristics and the device.

Apply Trial Evidence Without Ignoring Clinical VT

**MADIT-RIT tested high-rate or delayed-therapy programming against conventional programming in primary-prevention recipients.** It showed substantially less inappropriate therapy; the high-rate strategy also significantly reduced all-cause mortality in the original comparison.

This does not justify leaving known slower symptomatic VT outside detection zones. Secondary-prevention histories and drug-induced slowing of VT can require different settings.

Programming reduces unnecessary interventions but does not cure AF, repair a fractured lead or remove ventricular scar. Treat those problems in parallel. A monitor-only zone can help characterize selected rhythms, but should not replace treatment of a known dangerous episode. Review symptoms, syncope, therapies and remote monitoring after changes, and explain what the patient should do after shocks. Avoid interpreting a lower shock count as proof of absent arrhythmia without examining detection and episode data. The aim is dependable treatment of clinically consequential rhythms with fewer avoidable therapies, not simply minimizing a device counter at the expense of safety.

Shorten detection intervals to treat every brief fast rhythm sooner: Short detection can increase therapy for rhythms that would terminate spontaneously. Faster treatment is necessary for some dangerous rhythms, but is not a universal improvement.

Disable ATP so every detected ventricular episode receives a shock: ATP can painlessly terminate selected monomorphic VT. Removing it indiscriminately can increase shock burden without correcting inappropriate detection.

Raise the therapy threshold without reviewing stored rhythms or prior clinical VT: Higher cut-offs can reduce avoidable therapy in suitable populations, but can leave documented slower VT untreated. Programming must account for the actual clinical rhythm rather than applying one threshold blindly.

MADIT-RIT randomized programming trial, 2012 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1211107

EHRA multisociety electrical storm consensus, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1093/europace/euae049

questions.question: An alert patient receives recurrent ICD shocks while simultaneous monitored rhythm remains sinus at 82/min. Interrogation shows nonphysiological high-frequency ventricular signals consistent with lead noise. Which immediate strategy is most appropriate?
options: Apply a magnet and discharge once the shocks stop
Load amiodarone to suppress the presumed ventricular storm
Leave therapies active until a lead procedure can be completed
Suspend inappropriate tachytherapies under monitoring with external rescue available and arrange urgent device-system assessment
questions.explanation:
Recurrent ICD Shocks From Oversensing

Correct answer: Suspend inappropriate tachytherapies under monitoring with external rescue available and arrange urgent device-system assessment

Establish Whether Therapy Was Appropriate

**Stored electrograms and simultaneous clinical monitoring distinguish genuine ventricular arrhythmia from oversensing.** Lead noise, T-wave oversensing, electromagnetic interference and supraventricular rhythms can produce inappropriate detection.

A patient can remain conscious during real VT, so alertness alone does not establish inappropriate therapy. Here sinus rhythm during shocks and nonphysiological stored signals supply the stronger evidence.

Inspect sensing and impedance trends, lead integrity and relevant imaging or provoking circumstances through the device team. A normal single impedance value does not exclude an intermittent lead problem.

Stop Harm While Maintaining Rescue

**Temporarily inhibit inappropriate ICD therapies with programming or an appropriate magnet response while maintaining continuous monitoring and external defibrillation readiness.** Do not confuse therapy inhibition with correction of the cause.

An ICD magnet generally affects tachyarrhythmia detection or treatment rather than converting bradycardia pacing to an asynchronous mode. Manufacturer, model, programmed response and magnet position must be verified.

Arrange urgent electrophysiological/device-system review and the necessary lead or programming intervention. Reassess the patient after repeated shocks and provide analgesia or sedation when appropriate. If genuine VT/VF develops while internal therapies are disabled, external rescue must be immediately available. Restore a verified protective plan before leaving monitored care, and communicate any temporary settings to the receiving team. This differs from appropriate shocks during electrical storm, where sympathetic treatment, antiarrhythmics and ablation can be central. The first therapeutic distinction is whether the device is treating the patient’s arrhythmia or responding to a false signal; the same shock count can represent very different emergencies.

Apply a magnet and discharge once the shocks stop: A magnet may temporarily inhibit ICD tachytherapies, but does not resolve the lead fault. Response is device-specific, and inhibited protection requires supervised rescue capability and a definitive plan.

Load amiodarone to suppress the presumed ventricular storm: Antiarrhythmics can suppress true recurrent ventricular arrhythmias, but the recorded problem is false detection from lead noise. Drug loading does not repair the sensing fault and can add toxicity.

Leave therapies active until a lead procedure can be completed: Continued inappropriate shocks cause pain and can be dangerous. Temporary inhibition with reliable monitoring and external defibrillation support addresses the immediate harm while definitive correction is organized.

EHRA multisociety electrical storm consensus, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1093/europace/euae049

Multisociety ICD/CRT/pacing appropriate use criteria, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.023

questions.question: A patient with LVEF 30% soon after MI asks whether VEST proved that every patient awaiting primary-prevention reassessment should receive a wearable defibrillator. Which response is most accurate?
options: A secondary all-cause mortality finding establishes the primary arrhythmic endpoint as positive
VEST established a significant primary-endpoint benefit requiring universal post-MI use
VEST proved that a wearable device cannot terminate ventricular arrhythmia
VEST did not significantly reduce its primary arrhythmic-death endpoint in intention-to-treat analysis; temporary use requires individual assessment
questions.explanation:
Wearable Defibrillator Evidence After MI

Correct answer: VEST did not significantly reduce its primary arrhythmic-death endpoint in intention-to-treat analysis; temporary use requires individual assessment

Read the Prespecified Outcome and Treatment Exposure

**VEST randomized recent-MI patients with LVEF at most 35% to a wearable defibrillator plus medical treatment or medical treatment alone.** The main question concerned arrhythmic death during the early period before routine ICD eligibility.

Arrhythmic death occurred in 1.6% versus 2.4%, relative risk 0.67 with a 95% CI of 0.37–1.21. The primary intention-to-treat result was not statistically significant.

Median wear time was approximately eighteen hours daily and declined over follow-up. A device cannot provide protection while unworn, but adherence-based analyses are vulnerable to selection and cannot simply replace randomization.

Use Temporary Protection for a Defined Clinical Problem

**A wearable defibrillator can be considered selectively when transient risk or a temporary barrier to an indicated implanted device makes bridging useful.** Examples such as device extraction and early post-MI assessment have different evidence and circumstances.

It does not provide chronic pacing, ATP or CRT. Assess the patient’s ability and willingness to wear it, alarm handling, skin problems, inappropriate therapy risk and access to follow-up.

Continue GDMT and schedule EF and clinical reassessment rather than allowing a temporary device to postpone a durable decision indefinitely. An indicated ICD should not be replaced by indefinite wearable use solely because the vest can deliver shocks. Conversely, lack of a significant primary VEST result is not proof of no possible benefit in any selected bridging situation. Explain the trial’s uncertainty and the individual rationale explicitly. Review the date and purpose of reassessment, because recovery may remove a prophylactic indication while persistent qualifying dysfunction can support implantation. Device use supplements rather than replaces coronary treatment, HF optimization and prompt assessment of new syncope or sustained arrhythmia.

A secondary all-cause mortality finding establishes the primary arrhythmic endpoint as positive: Primary and secondary endpoints must remain distinct. An uncorrected secondary signal cannot be substituted for the prespecified primary result.

VEST established a significant primary-endpoint benefit requiring universal post-MI use: The primary arrhythmic-death comparison was not statistically significant. Selected temporary use should not be represented as a universal mandate derived from that trial.

VEST proved that a wearable device cannot terminate ventricular arrhythmia: A negative primary outcome does not mean the device cannot deliver an effective shock. Clinical effectiveness also depends on wear time, patient selection and competing causes of death.

  • VEST randomized recent-MI patients with LVEF at most 35% to a wearable defibrillator plus medical treatment or medical treatment alone. The main question concerned arrhythmic death during the early period before routine ICD eligibility.
    • Arrhythmic death occurred in 1.6% versus 2.4%, relative risk 0.67 with a 95% CI of 0.37–1.21. The primary intention-to-treat result was not statistically significant.
    • Median wear time was approximately eighteen hours daily and declined over follow-up. A device cannot provide protection while unworn, but adherence-based analyses are vulnerable to selection and cannot simply replace randomization.

Use Temporary Protection for a Defined Clinical Problem

  • A wearable defibrillator can be considered selectively when transient risk or a temporary barrier to an indicated implanted device makes bridging useful. Examples such as device extraction and early post-MI assessment have different evidence and circumstances.
    • It does not provide chronic pacing, ATP or CRT. Assess the patient’s ability and willingness to wear it, alarm handling, skin problems, inappropriate therapy risk and access to follow-up.
    • Continue GDMT and schedule EF and clinical reassessment rather than allowing a temporary device to postpone a durable decision indefinitely. An indicated ICD should not be replaced by indefinite wearable use solely because the vest can deliver shocks. Conversely, lack of a significant primary VEST result is not proof of no possible benefit in any selected bridging situation. Explain the trial’s uncertainty and the individual rationale explicitly. Review the date and purpose of reassessment, because recovery may remove a prophylactic indication while persistent qualifying dysfunction can support implantation. Device use supplements rather than replaces coronary treatment, HF optimization and prompt assessment of new syncope or sustained arrhythmia.

Other Options

  • A — A secondary all-cause mortality finding establishes the primary arrhythmic endpoint as positive: Primary and secondary endpoints must remain distinct. An uncorrected secondary signal cannot be substituted for the prespecified primary result.
  • B — VEST established a significant primary-endpoint benefit requiring universal post-MI use: The primary arrhythmic-death comparison was not statistically significant. Selected temporary use should not be represented as a universal mandate derived from that trial.
  • C — VEST proved that a wearable device cannot terminate ventricular arrhythmia: A negative primary outcome does not mean the device cannot deliver an effective shock. Clinical effectiveness also depends on wear time, patient selection and competing causes of death.

References

  • VEST randomized wearable-defibrillator trial, 2018
  • ESC ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death guideline, 2022
  • Multisociety ICD/CRT/pacing appropriate use criteria, 2025

questions.question: A 29-year-old dies suddenly during sleep. Expert autopsy and toxicology find no cause. The asymptomatic parents and siblings ask whether a normal routine ECG is sufficient to end investigation. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Use a broad genetic panel in each relative as a replacement for clinical screening
End family evaluation because a negative autopsy excludes inherited cardiac disease
Arrange multidisciplinary first-degree-relative screening and review of retained postmortem material, with phenotype-directed genetic counseling
Discharge all relatives permanently after one normal resting ECG
questions.explanation:
Family Evaluation After Unexplained Young Sudden Death

Correct answer: Arrange multidisciplinary first-degree-relative screening and review of retained postmortem material, with phenotype-directed genetic counseling

Investigate the Death and the Family Together

**Unexplained sudden death at a young age warrants expert review of the circumstances, autopsy, toxicology and available premortem records.** Retain suitable blood or tissue for postmortem molecular investigation when possible.

Obtain a three-generation pedigree, including unexplained drowning, seizure-like events, syncope, cardiomyopathy and premature pacemaker implantation. A death during sleep can be relevant but does not uniquely diagnose Brugada syndrome.

The 2020 APHRS/HRS consensus advises first-degree-relative screening after negative or absent autopsy when the decedent was younger than forty-five years, and with a clear phenotype regardless of age.

Use Clinical Screening and Genetics With Appropriate Interpretation

**Initial evaluation can include history, examination, ECG with high right-precordial leads, echocardiography and exercise testing.** Ambulatory monitoring, CMR and pharmacological provocation are selected according to the findings and specialist assessment.

When a pathogenic or likely pathogenic familial cause is identified, offer appropriately counseled cascade testing. A variant of uncertain significance must not be used as proof that a healthy relative has inherited a lethal disorder.

If no phenotype or causal result emerges, consider repeat clinical assessment rather than indiscriminate repeated broad genetic panels. The consensus recommends reassessment approximately every three to five years until at least age forty-five in selected unexplained young-death families, with timing adjusted for new symptoms or multiple events. A normal first screen is reassuring evidence, not a guarantee against later expression. Provide bereavement and psychological support alongside clear guidance on symptoms that require prompt review. Prevention decisions follow the identified disease and individual risk; family history alone does not automatically require an ICD in every relative. Preserve records and revisit variant interpretation or the pedigree when new evidence appears, because a later diagnosis in one member can clarify care for the entire family.

Use a broad genetic panel in each relative as a replacement for clinical screening: Unfocused testing can produce uncertain variants without identifying the cause. Clinical phenotype assessment and appropriate analysis of the decedent or an affected relative guide more interpretable testing.

End family evaluation because a negative autopsy excludes inherited cardiac disease: Primary electrical disorders may leave no structural autopsy finding, and early cardiomyopathy can be subtle. A negative autopsy does not establish absence of inherited susceptibility.

Discharge all relatives permanently after one normal resting ECG: A single ECG cannot exclude all concealed or age-dependent phenotypes. Initial screening uses complementary tests, and selected periodic re-evaluation may be needed when the cause remains unknown.

APHRS/HRS unexplained sudden death and family investigation consensus, 2020 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.hrthm.2020.10.010

ESC ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS genetic testing consensus, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1002/joa3.12717
